author: reek
body: The bundled agent is the path the USB-stick promise depends on: a person is handed a stick, boots it, and an agent is already there. AgentAcquisition named that path and answered it with a file-exists check and a `verified` field nobody ever set, so a bundled agent was indistinguishable from a directory with the right name in it. This chapter is the answer.

author: reek
body: The order matters and it is not the convenient one. Hashing is the expensive link and checking the signature first would let a stick full of noise cost only a signature verification. That is deliberate.

author: reek
body: **The foreign-format question is now answered in the read direction, and the answer is yes.** This chapter used to say that nothing established whether Codex could read a GGUF produced outside this tree, because the generator in `build/make-agent-bundle.ps1` writes the file and `Foreword chapter Gguf` reads it, and two halves written together agree whatever they both believe. That was the right caveat and it was wrong about one thing: it claimed there was no foreign model on this machine. There were ten.

author: reek
body: The manifest is line-oriented: a key, one space, the value, a newline. A key is only a key at the start of a line, so a value that happens to contain the word `sig` cannot be mistaken for the signature line.

author: reek
body: ab-value-offset answers where a key's value starts, or negative one when the key is absent. Negative one propagates rather than defaulting, because a missing field in a security manifest must refuse the bundle and not read as an empty value that then compares equal to something else empty.

author: reek
body: A hex run stops at the first byte that is not a hex digit rather than substituting a zero, so a truncated or corrupt key produces a short byte list that the length check below refuses. A silent zero would produce a well-formed-looking key of the right length that simply never verifies, which is a much harder thing to read off a failure.

author: reek
body: bundled-agent-verdict is the whole path: mount the boot volume, read the manifest, check the signature, check the digest, parse the model. Every step that can answer nothing answers a refusal naming the step, because a bundled agent that fails to load is a thing a person standing at a booted machine has to act on.

author: reek
body: The model is located rather than read. Its directory entry carries the length, which is compared against the manifest's claim before a single byte is hashed, so a model of the wrong size costs one lookup and not a scan. The sector-size check is here because the streaming digest below feeds whole 64-byte blocks out of each sector and carries no partial block between them, which is sound only while a sector is a whole number of blocks.

author: reek
body: The parse needs the bytes ahead of the tensor table and no others, and nothing announces how many that is until the walk has been made. So the walk is made over a window, and the window grows only on the evidence that it was too small. A window that already covers the whole file is not grown, because then a failed walk is a real answer about the file rather than about the window; that case falls through to the parse so the refusal names the actual link.

author: reek
body: The model is parsed far enough to prove it is one: a valid header, a metadata block the walk can step over, and a tensor table that yields a named tensor. Reaching the first tensor's name is the cheapest reading that a file of the right size full of the wrong bytes cannot produce. The size reported is the directory entry's and not the window's, because the window is an artefact of how the file was read and the person reading the verdict wants the model.

author: reek
body: The scan walks the model's cluster chain a sector at a time and never keeps a sector. Three things make that hold, and each of them is load-bearing:

author: reek
body: The eight hash words are ONE list, allocated before the mark. `sha256-compress` writes its result into the list it is given with `list-set-at` and returns that same list, so the words survive a rewind that reclaims everything else. A version of this loop that threaded a fresh eight-word list per block would allocate one per 64 bytes and defeat the whole exercise.

author: reek
body: The rewind happens at the TOP of each iteration rather than the bottom. The sector buffer, the message schedule, the sixty-four round records and the FAT sector that `fat16-next-cluster` reads are all allocated after the mark by the iteration that needs them, and all of them are gone before the next sector is read.

author: reek
body: The tail is the last chunk and only the last chunk. Every sector before it is full and a whole number of blocks, so no partial block is ever carried across a sector boundary; `ab-check-model` refuses a volume where that is not true rather than quietly hashing the wrong bytes. The padding is computed from the total length, not from the tail, which is what makes the answer identical to `sha256` over the same bytes.
